paras: The whipping of George Steitz was an attack on a Kenton County, Kentucky, man by about a dozen masked men on the night of Wednesday, August 22, 1888, at Clifton Heights, Kentucky. The men put a rope around his neck and pulled him up as if to hang him, then tied him to a tree, whipped him and released him. They acted because Steitz was alleged to have beaten his dying wife, and the one known report ran under the headline "Blue Grass White Caps."

The week before the attack, Steitz's wife died at St. Elizabeth's hospital in Covington after suffering from dropsy and paralysis. It was alleged that while she lay dying and "utterly helpless," her husband had beaten her "unmercifully." The report gives no race for Steitz or for the men who attacked him.

On Wednesday night about a dozen masked men came to Steitz's house and took him to a vacant house on Clifton Heights. There they placed a rope around his neck and pulled him up once or twice, "as if to hang him." Finally they tied him to a tree, gave him a thrashing and let him go.
No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the masked men was identified.

The story is known from a single Cincinnati dispatch dated August 25, which the Maysville Evening Bulletin printed on its front page that day among other short wire items. Under the headline "Blue Grass White Caps," the dispatch labeled the attackers whitecaps and treated the wife-beating as "alleged," yet still called Steitz "her brutal husband." It offered no comment on the masked men and no criticism of what they did. No other newspaper report of the attack was found.

reader.title: Whipping of George Steitz
bases: About a dozen masked men took Steitz from his home at night, staged a hanging, whipped him and let him go over an alleged offense against his wife, under the headline 'Blue Grass White Caps' (A1).

A masked band of about a dozen acting without legal authority punished Steitz for the alleged beating of his dying wife, but they pulled him up by a rope only 'as if to hang him', then whipped him and let him go; no one was killed (A1).
Only one report, a Cincinnati dispatch in the Maysville Evening Bulletin, was found (A1).
